title: Parents
tomorrow: one proverb praises a friend's love, another a friend's wounds. why?

lines: HE SPENDS SOME OF IT ON HER.
cards: A phone call that runs long because nobody wants to hang up first. A parent telling the same story again, and someone letting them finish. Now a harder scene, told gently.
Jesus on the cross, near the end. Below him stand the few who stayed: his mother among them, and the disciple he loved. He has almost nothing left to give.
And he spends some of it on her.

teach.b: John tells it this way: “When Jesus therefore saw his mother, and the disciple standing by, whom he loved, he saith unto his mother, Woman, behold thy son! Then saith he to the disciple, Behold thy mother! And from that hour that disciple took her unto his own home.”
Even there, he makes sure she has a home. The command behind it is old: “Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee.”
It comes with no age limit. A child honors by listening. A grown child honors in other ways.
Proverbs names the later season out loud: “Hearken unto thy father that begat thee, and despise not thy mother when she is old.” When she is old.
Here's the one to tell a friend tonight: in John's telling, one of Jesus' last acts is arranging care for his mother. So honor isn't only for the years when parents are strong and in charge.
It grows as they age: a longer call, a visit, patience with the same story, help with the forms.
Honor isn't the same as agreeing about everything, and it never means accepting harm. Some relationships with parents are hard or broken, and some parents have died.
Honor can still be a prayer, a memory kept well, or care for an elder who stood in a parent's place.

how: Christians honor parents in different seasons of life: obedience and listening as children, and later calls, visits, practical care and patience as parents age; where a parent has died, prayer and remembrance.

o: the leaders of a church who guide its members
the ones who raised us, honored more as they age
the oldest members of a family, and no one else

games.q: honor that grows — tap the pairs.
p: Jesus to the disciple he loved
honour thy father and thy mother
a command with no age limit

s: the command to honor parents ends when you grow up
Exodus gives no age limit, and Proverbs speaks of a mother when she is old.
in John, Jesus arranges a home for his mother from the cross
"from that hour that disciple took her unto his own home."
honoring parents means agreeing with them about everything
honor isn't agreement, and it never means accepting harm.

games.q: your mom tells the same story at dinner again. your brother groans, "we KNOW." what fits Proverbs 23:22?
o: correct her gently, so she stops repeating it.
let her finish, and ask her a question about it.
change the subject before she gets going.
games.why: "despise not thy mother when she is old." honor grows as parents age, and patience with the same story is one way it shows.

practice: Pick one elder, a parent, a grandparent, or someone who stood in that place, and write them a short message now: no news, just that you thought of them. Send it when you're ready, or if they've died, let it be a quiet thank-you.
Then sit with their face in mind.

wordCard.voice: Parents. The ones who raised us, or stood in that place, honored in ways that grow as they age.

orig.note: Hebrew: honor thy father and thy mother, Exodus 20:12.

carryVoice: Carry this: honor grows, from listening as a child to caring as they age. Day seventeen-sixteen.
